sections.title: The Thousand Years and the Final Defeat of Evil

blocks.text: Revelation 20 moves through the dragon's restraint, the reign of those who suffered for their witness, a final rebellion, and judgment before the great white throne. The text calls the martyrs' life and reign the first resurrection and contrasts it with the second death. It does not, by those phrases alone, settle every later dispute about the millennium or the precise sequencing and character of resurrection. Its narrative emphasis is that faithful witness is vindicated and evil finally loses its power to deceive and destroy.

Resurrection language belongs to a biblical hope in which God restores embodied life rather than merely describing the soul's escape from the world. In its ancient setting that claim stood apart from views that treated death as an irreversible descent or regarded bodily existence as something to leave behind. By the Second Temple period Jewish discussions included both developed resurrection expectation and disagreement about it, giving the chapter's scenes of life and judgment substantial theological force.

The names Gog and Magog place the last rebellion inside Revelation's sustained reuse of Ezekiel. The book does more than quote isolated verses: it recomposes images of throne, creatures, scroll, measuring, witness, plague, battle, city, river, and tree. Here that scriptural pattern portrays a worldwide assault that is abruptly ended by divine judgment, rather than offering a simple code for identifying one modern nation.

sections.title: A Vision Shaped by Israel's Scriptures

blocks.text: Across Revelation, images and phrases from Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, Zechariah, Genesis, and Psalms are taken up and rearranged. Reading chapter 20 within that scriptural world keeps its symbolism connected to earlier stories of oppression, deliverance, judgment, and restored creation. It also cautions against treating each image as a freestanding timetable marker detached from the book's larger vision.
